clue.text: The Fleet Street crowd

parts.note: Fleet Street in London was long the home of Britain's national newspapers, so its crowd is the body of journalists collectively, also a word for a throng

explanation.surface: A description of the gang of journalists who once worked on London's newspaper street.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street is the London street where the national papers had their offices; the collective name for journalists is also a verb and noun meaning to crowd or a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers and their reporters are collectively known by this word, which also means a dense throng of people.

clue.text: Element which symbolically appears all right with oxygen

definitions.text: Element which symbolically appears all right with oxygen

parts.words: Element which symbolically appears all right with oxygen
parts.note: the element's chemical symbol K, placed after O for oxygen, spells OK, meaning all right

explanation.surface: A chemistry riddle about an element that looks fine when paired with oxygen.
explanation.walkthrough: Chemical symbols: O is oxygen, K the element sought; O and K together read OK, 'all right'.
explanation.definitionFit: This soft alkali metal is a chemical element whose symbol is K.

clue.text: Delete article written in a form of Gaelic

indicators.note: written in means one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: Erse is Irish or Scottish Gaelic
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Removing a newspaper piece composed in Gaelic.
explanation.walkthrough: ERSE is an old name for Gaelic; A goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To wipe out or rub off something is to delete it.

clue.text: Church feature quietly accepted by producer of The Tatler

indicators.note: accepted by means taken inside the other piece

parts.note: Richard Steele founded the 18th-century periodical The Tatler
p is piano, the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: A church tower quietly approved by the publisher of a society magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Richard Steele launched The Tatler in 1709; P (piano, quiet) goes inside his name.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall spire-topped tower is a familiar part of a church building.

clue.text: No dogs are troubling this bird

indicators.note: troubling suggests disturbing the letters of the phrase no dogs are into a new order

explanation.surface: An observation that the dogs present are not bothering a particular bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubling' rearranges the nine letters of NO DOGS ARE.
explanation.definitionFit: A goosander is a species of sawbill duck, a kind of bird.

clue.text: Hers is, we hear, not the least effective

definitions.text: Hers is, we hear, not the least effective

parts.words: Hers is, we hear, not the least effective
parts.note: her knot, which sounds like not, is the badly tied reef knot that slips, so it is not effective

explanation.surface: A remark that someone's efforts are reportedly not the most effective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' heard as 'knot': a granny knot is a reef knot tied the wrong way, which slips.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandmother lends her name to a faulty, slipping knot.

clue.text: Fruit tree the other way round this day in May

indicators.note: the other way round means the two pieces are placed in reverse of their clue order

parts.note: an oak is a tree
an apple is a fruit

explanation.surface: A fruit tree turned around on a particular spring day.
explanation.walkthrough: Oak Apple Day, 29 May, commemorated Charles II's restoration and his hiding in an oak tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The 29 May holiday celebrating the Restoration of Charles II took its name from the oak gall.

clue.text: A place for birds to nest of course

parts.note: birds nest in a tree, so the place is in tree

explanation.surface: Somewhere for birds to build their nests, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but points to a racecourse, home of the Grand National near Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: This racecourse near Liverpool hosts the Grand National steeplechase.

clue.text: Craftily enlist aid to take property out of settlement

indicators.note: craftily suggests the letters of enlist aid are cunningly rearranged

explanation.surface: Cunningly recruiting help to free land from an inheritance arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craftily' rearranges ENLIST AID; an entail restricts who may inherit an estate.
explanation.definitionFit: To free an estate from an entail, a legal restriction on inheritance, is the legal sense meant.

clue.text: Mathematical problem for Lady Godiva for instance

definitions.meaning: a subsidiary problem added to a theorem in geometry
she famously rode naked on horseback through Coventry, so she was a horsewoman

explanation.surface: A maths puzzle about a famous naked horsewoman.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Godiva is the legendary noblewoman who rode naked through Coventry.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an extra exercise in geometry and someone on horseback.

clue.text: Manufacturer's device to exchange foreign currency

parts.note: to exchange goods is to trade them
the mark was the currency of Germany

explanation.surface: A suggestion that a firm's emblem is a way of swapping money abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The MARK was Germany's currency before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: A registered symbol or name that identifies a maker's goods is the device meant here.

clue.text: Cautiously advanced issue rejected by editor

indicators.note: rejected means the word for issue is turned back to front

parts.note: issue means offspring, a son

explanation.surface: A newspaper story spiked by the editor after being put forward hesitantly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' looks like a matter or edition, given the editor, but here it means a child.
explanation.definitionFit: To edge forward carefully, as a car does into traffic, is to have moved in that way.

clue.text: Is he unconsciously involved in the business?

definitions.text: Is he unconsciously involved in the business?

parts.words: Is he unconsciously involved in the business?
parts.note: the image is of someone asleep while still being part of a firm, the term for an investor with no active role

explanation.surface: A question about whether a man is drifting into a business without knowing it.
explanation.definitionFit: An investor who puts money into a firm but takes no part in running it is described literally as dozing.

clue.text: One pair of boys given a 1 ac

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
Ron is a boy's name, the first of the pair
Ed is a boy's name, the second of the pair

explanation.surface: A cross-reference saying a couple of lads received something from another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 ac' means the answer to 1 across, a word for smoothing clothes with a hot iron; the definition is the past participle.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes that have been smoothed with a hot flat appliance have been given that treatment.

clue.text: Forthright verdict as given by umpire

definitions.meaning: the umpire's verdict out, when spoken aloud by him

explanation.surface: An umpire's blunt decision on a cricket field.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the umpire's verdict against a batsman is 'out', and it is spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Being blunt and frank, and the umpire's call voiced, both fit the word.

clue.text: Lose the favour of a foreign goddess

parts.note: alien means foreign
Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and ruin

explanation.surface: Someone falling out of favour with a goddess from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: ATE, Greek goddess of folly, is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange someone is to cause them to stop feeling friendly towards you.

clue.text: How rain falls to form hard water

indicators.note: to form signals the letters of hard water are shaped into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Rain coming down to turn into water rich in minerals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to form' rearranges HARD WATER.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain moves down towards the ground, in that direction.

clue.text: A halo — or a Cockney's untidy lumber-room?

definitions.meaning: a ring of light round a saint's head
a cubbyhole full of junk, said in Cockney style with the h dropped

explanation.surface: A question whether a saint's ring of light is really a London junk room.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys drop their H, so 'glory hole' (a messy storeroom) becomes 'glory 'ole'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a small aureole of light, and also a dropped-h rendering of a junk cupboard.

clue.text: Protect against attack by future night-fliers

definitions.text: Protect against attack by future night-fliers

parts.words: Protect against attack by future night-fliers
parts.note: the night-fliers are moths, and their future generations are the larvae that eat clothes, kept off by small balls of repellent

explanation.surface: Defence against a raid by aircraft that have yet to take off at night.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'night-fliers' sound like bombers, but they are moths whose larvae eat stored clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To store something away with repellent balls, or figuratively shelve it, guards it against moth grubs.

clue.text: Sir Thomas, writer about one sort of household help

indicators.note: about means wrapped round the other piece

parts.note: Sir Thomas Browne was a 17th-century English writer, author of Religio Medici
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: An author writing about a kind of domestic helper.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Thomas Browne wrote Religio Medici; I goes inside his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore a helpful goblin secretly does chores around the house at night.

clue.text: Said to be the vendor of a wine-store

indicators.note: said to be signals a word that sounds like another when spoken

parts.note: a vendor is a seller

explanation.surface: A remark that a man is supposedly the trader behind a wine shop.
explanation.definitionFit: An underground room where bottles are kept is a store for wine.

clue.text: Reversion of property points to a swindler

parts.note: E and S are compass points, east and south
a cheat is a swindler

explanation.surface: Property returning to its owner thanks to a fraudster's tips.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points E and S come first.
explanation.definitionFit: Land passing back to the Crown or lord when an owner dies without heirs is the legal term.

clue.text: Investments frame-up exposing one to ridicule

definitions.meaning: shares and securities held as investments
a wooden frame set up to lock an offender's legs for public mockery

explanation.surface: Investments described as a set-up meant to humiliate someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frame-up' looks like a fabricated charge; it is a frame set up, the old wooden punishment device.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers shares held, and the wooden frame in which offenders were pilloried.

clue.text: Doctors observe river horse and chariot act mix-up

parts.note: hippopotamus is Greek for river horse, shortened to hippo

indicators.note: mix-up means the letters of chariot act are jumbled

explanation.surface: Medics watching a muddled circus act involving a hippo and a chariot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mix-up' rearranges CHARIOT ACT into CRATICOATH; 'river horse' is the literal Greek meaning of hippopotamus.
explanation.definitionFit: The pledge of medical ethics named after an ancient Greek physician is something doctors keep.

clue.text: What Edmund Spenser in 'part abhorred

indicators.note: in part signals that the letters lie within a part of the words what Edmund

explanation.surface: Something the Elizabethan poet partly detested.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'wHAT EDmund'; Spenser is the Elizabethan poet, there for the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Loathed or detested is the sense of the past tense here.

clue.text: Bloomer causes teacher to lose his head

indicators.note: lose his head means the first letter of the teacher's word is removed

parts.note: a schoolmaster is a teacher

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster's embarrassing mistake makes him lose his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a blunder, but it is a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A flowering garden plant is something that blooms.

clue.text: A sign "To the Field of Knowledge

parts.note: ken means range of knowledge or understanding

explanation.surface: A signpost pointing the way to a field called Knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: KEN means one's range of knowledge, as in 'beyond my ken'.
explanation.definitionFit: A symbol or mark that stands for something is a sign.

clue.text: Box with odd Scottish covering — part of the old theatre

indicators.note: covering means one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: orra is a Scots word for odd or spare
a chest is a box

explanation.surface: A box wrapped in strange Scottish material, an item from a historic playhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: ORRA is a Scots word few solvers know; 'Box' wants to be a theatre box, but it is the container being covered.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greek theatres the semicircular space in front of the stage where the chorus danced bore this name.

clue.text: Being close together makes sense in retreats

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: dens are retreats or hideaways

indicators.note: makes signals the word sense being made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A claim that crowding together is the sensible thing to do in hideaways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' rearranges SENSE into SENES before it goes in; 'makes sense' reads as an idiom but splits into indicator and fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Compactness or thickness of packing is the quality of things crowded tightly.

clue.text: It turns colour, once dressed

indicators.note: turns signals that the word it is reversed

parts.note: red is a colour

explanation.surface: Something changes colour after it has been clothed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' makes TI from IT; 'once' marks the archaic sense of attired.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage, to be attired, clothed, was expressed by this shortened form.
